problems.title: Gauge to absolute pressure
problems.scenario:
A tyre-pressure gauge reads **220 kPa**. The local atmospheric pressure is $P_{\text{atm}} = 100\ \text{kPa}$.

What is the **absolute pressure** in the tyre?
hints: A gauge reads pressure *relative* to the atmosphere.
$P_{\text{abs}} = P_{\text{atm}} + P_{\text{gage}}$.
problems.solution:
A gauge measures how far above atmospheric the pressure sits, so convert by adding the atmospheric value:

$$P_{\text{abs}} = P_{\text{atm}} + P_{\text{gage}} = 100 + 220 = 320\ \text{kPa}$$

Always do this conversion before using a pressure in any property relation or gas law — those require **absolute** pressure.

problems.title: Vacuum to absolute pressure
problems.scenario:
A vacuum gauge on a condenser reads **30 kPa**, while the atmosphere is at $P_{\text{atm}} = 98\ \text{kPa}$.

Find the **absolute pressure** inside the condenser.
hints: A vacuum gauge reads how far *below* atmospheric the pressure is.
$P_{\text{abs}} = P_{\text{atm}} - P_{\text{vac}}$.
problems.solution:
A vacuum reading is measured downward from atmospheric, so subtract it:

$$P_{\text{abs}} = P_{\text{atm}} - P_{\text{vac}} = 98 - 30 = 68\ \text{kPa}$$

The absolute pressure is below atmospheric, as expected for a vacuum.

problems.title: Density and specific volume
problems.scenario:
A rigid tank of volume $0.50\ \text{m}^3$ holds **0.60 kg** of a gas.

Find the **specific volume** of the gas.
hints: Specific volume is volume per unit mass.
$v = V/m$ (and it equals $1/\rho$).
problems.solution:
Specific volume is simply the volume occupied by each kilogram:

$$v = \frac{V}{m} = \frac{0.50\ \text{m}^3}{0.60\ \text{kg}} = 0.833\ \text{m}^3/\text{kg}$$

The density is the reciprocal, $\rho = 1/v = 1.20\ \text{kg/m}^3$.

problems.title: Pressure at depth in water
problems.scenario:
A diver is **8.0 m** below the surface of a lake. Water density is $\rho = 1000\ \text{kg/m}^3$ and the surface is at atmospheric pressure $P_{\text{atm}} = 101\ \text{kPa}$. Take $g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Find the **absolute pressure** acting on the diver.
hints: Pressure rises with depth by $\rho g h$.
$P = P_{\text{atm}} + \rho g h$. Careful with units: $\rho g h$ comes out in Pa.
Divide the $\rho g h$ term by 1000 to convert Pa → kPa.
problems.solution:
Add the hydrostatic column to the surface pressure:

$$P = P_{\text{atm}} + \rho g h$$

The depth term:

$$\rho g h = 1000 \times 9.81 \times 8.0 = 78\,480\ \text{Pa} = 78.5\ \text{kPa}$$

So:

$$P = 101 + 78.5 = 179.5\ \text{kPa}$$

problems.title: Hydraulic lift
problems.scenario:
A hydraulic lift has a small input piston of area $A_1 = 0.010\ \text{m}^2$ and a large output piston of area $A_2 = 0.40\ \text{m}^2$. A car rests on the large piston, pressing down with a force of **5000 N**.

What **input force** $F_1$ must be applied to the small piston to balance it?
hints: The pressure is the same throughout the connected fluid (Pascal's principle).
Rearrange: $F_1 = F_2\,(A_1/A_2)$.
problems.solution:
Both pistons share the same fluid pressure, so $F_1/A_1 = F_2/A_2$. Rearranging for the input force:

$$F_1 = F_2\,\frac{A_1}{A_2} = 5000 \times \frac{0.010}{0.40} = 5000 \times 0.025 = 125\ \text{N}$$

The large area multiplies force by 40×, which is why a small input lifts a heavy car.

problems.title: Gas pressure under a loaded piston
problems.scenario:
A vertical piston–cylinder contains gas. The piston has a mass of **20 kg** and a face area of $A = 0.012\ \text{m}^2$. The atmosphere above pushes down at $P_{\text{atm}} = 100\ \text{kPa}$. Take $g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Find the **absolute gas pressure** inside the cylinder.
hints: Do a force balance on the piston: the gas below supports the atmosphere plus the piston's weight.
$P_{\text{gas}}A = P_{\text{atm}}A + mg$, so $P_{\text{gas}} = P_{\text{atm}} + mg/A$.
$mg/A$ is in Pa — divide by 1000 for kPa.
problems.solution:
Balance the forces on the piston. The gas pressure below must support both the atmospheric push and the piston's weight:

$$P_{\text{gas}}A = P_{\text{atm}}A + mg \quad\Rightarrow\quad P_{\text{gas}} = P_{\text{atm}} + \frac{mg}{A}$$

The weight term:

$$\frac{mg}{A} = \frac{20 \times 9.81}{0.012} = \frac{196.2}{0.012} = 16\,350\ \text{Pa} = 16.35\ \text{kPa}$$

Therefore:

$$P_{\text{gas}} = 100 + 16.35 = 116.35\ \text{kPa}$$

problems.title: Multi-fluid manometer
problems.scenario:
A pressurised gas tank is connected to a tube open to the atmosphere ($P_{\text{atm}} = 100\ \text{kPa}$). Walking from the gas surface to the open end, you go **down** a column of oil (SG = 0.72) of height **0.20 m**, then the tube bends and goes **up** a column of mercury (SG = 13.6) of height **0.30 m**.

Find the **absolute gas pressure**. Take $\rho_{\text{water}} = 1000\ \text{kg/m}^3$, $g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2$.
hints: Use the manometer 'walking' rule: add $\rho g h$ going **down** a column, subtract it going **up**.
Density from specific gravity: $\rho = SG \times 1000$. Oil: 720 kg/m³; mercury: 13 600 kg/m³.
$P_{\text{gas}} + \rho_{oil}g h_{oil} - \rho_{Hg}g h_{Hg} = P_{\text{atm}}$. Solve for $P_{\text{gas}}$.
problems.solution:
Walk from the gas to the open end, adding $\rho g h$ when descending and subtracting when ascending, ending at atmospheric pressure:

$$P_{\text{gas}} + \rho_{oil}\,g\,h_{oil} - \rho_{Hg}\,g\,h_{Hg} = P_{\text{atm}}$$

Solve for the gas pressure:

$$P_{\text{gas}} = P_{\text{atm}} - \rho_{oil}\,g\,h_{oil} + \rho_{Hg}\,g\,h_{Hg}$$

Evaluate each column (using $\rho = SG \times 1000$):

$$\rho_{oil}\,g\,h_{oil} = 720 \times 9.81 \times 0.20 = 1413\ \text{Pa} = 1.41\ \text{kPa}$$

$$\rho_{Hg}\,g\,h_{Hg} = 13\,600 \times 9.81 \times 0.30 = 40\,025\ \text{Pa} = 40.02\ \text{kPa}$$

$$P_{\text{gas}} = 100 - 1.41 + 40.02 = 138.6\ \text{kPa}$$

problems.title: Mercury differential manometer
problems.scenario:
A horizontal pipe carries **water** ($\rho = 1000\ \text{kg/m}^3$). A mercury (SG = 13.6) differential manometer is connected between two points at the **same elevation**, and the mercury level difference is **0.45 m**. Take $g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Find the **pressure difference** $P_1 - P_2$ between the two points.
hints: For a differential manometer between two taps at equal elevation with a heavier measuring fluid, the connecting-fluid columns cancel.
$P_1 - P_2 = (\rho_{Hg} - \rho_{water})\,g\,h$.
Use $\rho_{Hg} = 13\,600$ and $\rho_{water} = 1000\ \text{kg/m}^3$.
problems.solution:
When the two pressure taps are at the same height and the manometer fluid (mercury) is heavier than the line fluid (water), the water columns on each side cancel and only the *difference* in densities matters:

$$P_1 - P_2 = (\rho_{Hg} - \rho_{water})\,g\,h$$

Substitute:

$$P_1 - P_2 = (13\,600 - 1000) \times 9.81 \times 0.45 = 12\,600 \times 9.81 \times 0.45$$

$$P_1 - P_2 = 55\,623\ \text{Pa} = 55.6\ \text{kPa}$$

Using the large density contrast of mercury keeps the column height manageable for a sizeable pressure difference.

problems.title: Two-fluid pressure difference in a tank
problems.scenario:
A vertical cylindrical container is **6.0 m** tall. Its **lower half** is filled with water ($\rho = 1000\ \text{kg/m}^3$) and its **upper half** with oil (SG = 0.85). Take $g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Find the **pressure difference** between the very top and the very bottom of the container.
hints: Split the column into its two fluid layers — each contributes its own $\rho g h$.
Each layer is half the height: $h = 3.0\ \text{m}$.
Total: $\Delta P = \rho_{oil}gh + \rho_{water}gh$.
problems.solution:
The total pressure difference is the sum of the hydrostatic contributions of each 3.0 m layer:

$$\Delta P = \rho_{oil}\,g\,h + \rho_{water}\,g\,h$$

With $\rho_{oil} = 0.85\times1000 = 850\ \text{kg/m}^3$ and $h = 3.0\ \text{m}$ for each layer:

$$\Delta P = (850\times9.81\times3.0) + (1000\times9.81\times3.0) = 25\,015.5 + 29\,430 = 54\,445\ \text{Pa}$$

$$\Delta P \approx 54.4\ \text{kPa}$$

Each layer is independent — you can't just use the *average* density over the full 6 m, because the layers don't mix; add each layer's contribution separately.

problems.title: Doubling the pressure with added weights
problems.scenario:
A vertical piston–cylinder device contains gas at **100 kPa**. The piston has a mass of **10 kg** and a diameter of **14 cm**. Take $g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Weights are placed on the piston to **double** the gas pressure to 200 kPa. Find the **mass of the weights** needed, in kg. (As an intermediate step, you'll need the local atmospheric pressure.)
hints: First find the atmospheric pressure from the *initial* force balance: $P_1 = P_{\text{atm}} + m_{piston}g/A$.
The piston area is $A = \pi D^2/4$.
Then redo the force balance at $P_2 = 200\ \text{kPa}$ with the *combined* mass of piston + weights, and solve for the weights' mass.
problems.solution:
**Step 1 — find the atmospheric pressure.** The piston area is:

$$A = \frac{\pi D^2}{4} = \frac{\pi (0.14)^2}{4} = 0.01539\ \text{m}^2$$

The initial force balance on the piston gives:

$$P_1 = P_{\text{atm}} + \frac{m_{piston}g}{A} \;\Rightarrow\; P_{\text{atm}} = 100 - \frac{10\times9.81}{0.01539}\times10^{-3} = 100 - 6.37 = 93.6\ \text{kPa}$$

**Step 2 — solve for the added mass.** Doubling the pressure to $P_2 = 200\ \text{kPa}$ needs a new force balance with both masses:

$$P_2 = P_{\text{atm}} + \frac{(m_{piston}+m_w)g}{A}$$

$$m_{piston}+m_w = \frac{(P_2 - P_{\text{atm}})\times10^3\times A}{g} = \frac{(200-93.6)\times10^3\times0.01539}{9.81} = 167.0\ \text{kg}$$

$$m_w = 167.0 - 10 = 157\ \text{kg}$$

The key move is realising you need **two** force balances — one to back out the unknown atmospheric pressure, a second to find the unknown added weight.

problems.title: Helium balloon: buoyancy and acceleration
problems.scenario:
A helium balloon is a sphere of diameter **12 m**, carrying two people of **85 kg** each (neglect the ropes and cage). Air density is $\rho_{air} = 1.16\ \text{kg/m}^3$; helium density is $\rho_{He} = \rho_{air}/7$. Take $g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2$.

The buoyancy force is $F_b = \rho_{air}\,g\,V_{balloon}$. Find the **upward acceleration** of the balloon the instant it is released.
hints: First find the balloon's volume: $V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ with $r = 6\ \text{m}$.
The net upward force is buoyancy minus *everything* being lifted: the helium's own weight and the people's weight.
Newton's second law: $a = F_{net}/m_{total}$, where $m_{total}$ is the mass actually being accelerated (helium gas + people).
problems.solution:
**Volume of the balloon:**

$$V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \frac{4}{3}\pi(6)^3 = 904.8\ \text{m}^3$$

**Forces.** Buoyancy from the displaced air:

$$F_b = \rho_{air}\,g\,V = 1.16\times9.81\times904.8 = 10\,296\ \text{N}$$

Weight of the helium filling the balloon ($\rho_{He} = 1.16/7 = 0.1657\ \text{kg/m}^3$):

$$W_{He} = \rho_{He}\,g\,V = 0.1657\times9.81\times904.8 = 1471\ \text{N}$$

Weight of the two people:

$$W_{people} = 2\times85\times9.81 = 1668\ \text{N}$$

**Net force and acceleration.** The net upward force is:

$$F_{net} = F_b - W_{He} - W_{people} = 10\,296 - 1471 - 1668 = 7157\ \text{N}$$

The accelerating mass is the helium gas plus the people (the balloon *displaces* the air, but doesn't carry its mass):

$$m_{total} = \rho_{He}V + 2(85) = 149.9 + 170 = 319.9\ \text{kg}$$

$$a = \frac{F_{net}}{m_{total}} = \frac{7157}{319.9} = 22.4\ \text{m/s}^2$$
